title: Attention is love
hook: Simone Weil held that attention is the rarest, purest form of generosity

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Waldinger, and the Harvard study's headline: close relationships. Your line was relationships. Today closes the week with a gift any relationship can use.

Two people at a café table. One is telling a story that matters to her: a diagnosis in the family, a fear she hasn't said out loud before. The other is nodding, saying mm-hm, and glancing every few seconds at the phone face-up beside the coffee. Nothing rude has been said. Nobody has left. And still something is missing from that table, and both of them can feel it. A French philosopher named Simone Weil had a word for what's missing, and she ranked it very high among the things one person can give another.
screen: `A STORY THAT MATTERS.` → `A GLANCE AT THE PHONE.` → `SOMETHING IS MISSING.`

segments.voice: In a letter to a friend, Simone Weil wrote that attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity. Not money, not advice, not even kind words. Attention. One way to read her: rare because it's hard to give, pure because it asks nothing back. In an essay on school studies, she describes students who think they're paying attention because they frown and tense their muscles. That isn't it, she says. Real attention is closer to waiting: the mind emptied, open, ready to receive what's actually there, instead of rushing in with its own ideas. In that same essay, she says that love of neighbor, in its fullness, means being able to ask someone what they are going through, and to really look at the person suffering, not as a case or an example, but as a human being exactly like ourselves. Weil, who was deeply drawn to Christianity, believed this kind of attention was close to prayer. But you don't need her faith to try it. Back at the café table, it might look like turning the phone face-down, and letting the other person's story be the only thing in the room. It costs nothing but ourselves.
screen: `THE RAREST, PUREST GENEROSITY.` · `NOT STRAINING, BUT WAITING.` · `WHAT ARE YOU GOING THROUGH?` · `THE PHONE FACE-DOWN.` · then, large: `ATTENTION IS LOVE.`

segments.voice: Practice the waiting kind of attention on one simple thing in front of you, your breath, a sound in the room, the light on a wall, without gripping it or frowning at it, letting it come to you the way you'd wait for someone to finish a sentence. When your mind runs ahead, notice, and come back to waiting; then, before the bell, bring to mind one person who could use five minutes of this attention from you.
Simone Weil. The French philosopher who called attention the rarest and purest form of generosity, close to love itself. Today's word.

Your line: what they are going through. That ends a week of love's names: gladness, an even heart, ren, care for other people's families, a home port, relationships, and now attention. Seven days, seven names.

howItsDone: Readers of Simone Weil practice attention as a kind of open, patient waiting: setting aside distractions to listen fully to another person, which she linked to love of neighbor and to prayer.
